actions.justification: Mandatory first step: Patient with CKD stage 4 and diabetes is at high risk for contrast-induced nephropathy. Assessing hydration status guides pre-procedural IV fluid administration to protect the kidneys.
Mandatory: Baseline eGFR must be established before contrast administration in a CKD stage 4 patient to quantify nephropathy risk and guide contrast volume limits and prophylactic measures.
Mandatory: Patient has CKD stage 4 and diabetes, both major risk factors for contrast-induced nephropathy. Formal risk factor review guides the overall prevention strategy.

Patient has CKD stage 4 and diabetes undergoing cardiac catheterization - baseline vital signs assessment is critical before contrast exposure to establish hemodynamic stability and guide pre-procedural optimization.
Review current medications to identify nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, metformin, ACE inhibitors) that may need to be held before contrast administration in this high-risk CKD/diabetes patient.

This patient with CKD stage 4 and diabetes is at high risk for contrast-induced nephropathy. Calculating maximum safe contrast volume limit (based on eGFR) is essential before cardiac catheterization to minimize AKI risk.

Patient has CKD stage 4 and diabetes — both high-risk features for contrast-induced AKI. Nephrology consultation is indicated pre-procedure to optimize kidney protection strategy and guide peri-procedural management.

Given CKD stage 4 and diabetes, consider whether the cardiac catheterization can be performed with reduced contrast or whether alternative non-contrast imaging modalities (e.g., cardiac MRI, CT without contrast) could provide equivalent diagnostic information with less nephrotoxic risk.

CKD stage 4 patients are highly vulnerable to AKI. Holding NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, and other nephrotoxic agents peri-procedurally is a key guideline-recommended intervention to reduce contrast-induced nephropathy risk.

Patient has CKD stage 4 and diabetes with planned contrast exposure; discontinuing nephrotoxic agents (e.g., NSAIDs, metformin) before catheterization reduces risk of contrast-induced nephropathy per standard guidelines.
Document the baseline eGFR result to establish reference point for post-procedure comparison and to confirm risk stratification for contrast-induced AKI in this CKD stage 4 patient.
Assessing urine output ensures adequate pre-procedural hydration status and serves as an early indicator of renal perfusion in this high-risk patient prior to contrast administration.

Patient has CKD stage 4 and diabetes. Metformin should be held before contrast administration due to risk of lactic acidosis, per standard guidelines for diabetic patients undergoing contrast procedures.

Pre-procedure IV hydration with isotonic crystalloid is a cornerstone of contrast-induced nephropathy (CIN) prevention in high-risk patients (CKD stage 4 + diabetes). Begin IV fluid administration prior to catheterization.
Patient has CKD stage 4; review and adjust renally-dosed medications as needed prior to procedure to minimize additional nephrotoxic burden.

Patient has CKD stage 4 and is undergoing cardiac catheterization with contrast exposure. Holding nephrotoxic medications (e.g., NSAIDs, aminoglycosides) is critical to reduce risk of contrast-induced nephropathy in this high-risk patient.

Pre- and post-contrast IV hydration with isotonic crystalloid is a cornerstone of CI-AKI prevention in high-risk patients (CKD stage 4 + diabetes). Ensure adequate hydration protocol is planned for post-procedure period.
Patient has CKD stage 4 (likely GFR <30, G3b or worse) and is receiving contrast. Metformin should be held due to risk of lactic acidosis in the setting of potential contrast-induced AKI.

Patient has CKD stage 4 and diabetes, placing them at high risk for contrast-induced nephropathy. Pre-procedural IV hydration with isotonic crystalloid is a cornerstone of CI-AKI prevention prior to cardiac catheterization.
Ongoing urine output monitoring is essential in this high-risk patient (CKD stage 4, diabetes) to assess renal perfusion adequacy before and after contrast exposure.
Serial serum creatinine measurement at 48-72 hours post-contrast is recommended to detect contrast-induced AKI, as peak creatinine rise typically occurs in this window.

Patient with CKD stage 4 and diabetes undergoing cardiac catheterization with contrast is at high risk for contrast-induced nephropathy. Serum creatinine at 48 hours post-contrast is the standard monitoring timepoint to detect AKI.
Serial creatinine monitoring at 72 hours post-contrast provides additional assessment for delayed contrast-induced nephropathy in this high-risk patient with CKD stage 4 and diabetes.
Optimizing fluid status in a CKD stage 4 diabetic patient pre/peri-catheterization helps mitigate risk of contrast-induced nephropathy by maintaining adequate renal perfusion.
